Cause-specific structural nested cumulative survival time models for competing risks, with application to the Antibody Mediated Prevention trials

Yuxiao Li ††thanks: The first two authors contributed equally. Affiliation: Department of Statistics, University of Washington    Yuhao Deng∗ Affiliation: Vaccine and Infectious Disease Division, Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center    Bo Zhang ††thanks: Assistant Professor of Biostatistics, Vaccine and Infectious Disease Division, Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center. Email: bzhang3@fredhutch.org. Affiliation: Vaccine and Infectious Disease Division, Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center
Abstract

The Antibody Mediated Prevention (AMP) trials randomized participants to VRC01, a broadly neutralizing antibody, or placebo; the primary analysis estimated prevention efficacy against overall HIV-1 acquisition and against acquisition of VRC01-sensitive strains. All participants were offered daily oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), and PrEP uptake in a trial may differ substantially from uptake in other settings. It is therefore of interest to estimate the effect of oral PrEP on acquisition of VRC01-sensitive and VRC01-insensitive strains, as well as the counterfactual cumulative incidence of such acquisition under no or limited PrEP uptake. To address these questions, we extend the structural nested cumulative survival time model (SNCSTM), a causal survival model for time-varying treatments, to a cause-specific version. We show that the cause-specific SNCSTM is closely related to the Fine–Gray subdistribution hazard model, and we study identification under two frameworks. The first, based on sequential ignorability, applies when the time-varying treatment is distinct from the randomized assignment, as with oral PrEP use in AMP. The second, based on an instrumental variable, applies when the time-varying treatment represents compliance with the randomized assignment, and it accommodates unmeasured confounding between the time-varying treatment and event time. Under both frameworks, we propose consistent and asymptotically normal estimators of the structural parameters. We apply the methods to HVTN 704/HPTN 085, one of the two AMP trials, to estimate the effects of oral PrEP use and of VRC01 infusions administered every 8 weeks on acquisition of VRC01-sensitive and VRC01-insensitive HIV-1 strains. We also estimate the counterfactual strain-specific cumulative incidence curves under no oral PrEP use and under full adherence to the scheduled VRC01 infusions.

Keywords: Fine–Gray competing risk model; G-estimation; Subdistribution hazard; Sequential ignorability; Instrumental variable.

1 Introduction

1.1 The Antibody Mediated Prevention trials

The Antibody Mediated Prevention (AMP) trials (HVTN 703/HPTN 081 and HVTN 704/HPTN 085) were a pair of landmark Phase 2b, randomized, placebo-controlled HIV prevention studies designed to test whether VRC01, a CD4-binding site (CD4bs)-targeting broadly neutralizing monoclonal antibody (bnAb), could prevent HIV-1 acquisition. VRC01 was administered as an intravenous infusion every eight weeks to HIV-uninfected individuals at elevated risk of infection (Corey et al., 2021). HVTN 704/HPTN 085 enrolled cisgender men and transgender women who have sex with men in the Americas and Europe, whereas HVTN 703/HPTN 081 enrolled cisgender women in sub-Saharan Africa. Participants were randomized to one of three arms: placebo, VRC01 at 10 mg per kilogram (low-dose arm), or VRC01 at 30 mg per kilogram (high-dose arm). The study found VRC01 did not significantly reduce overall HIV-1 acquisition compared with placebo (prevention efficacy [PE]: 26.6%; 95% confidence interval [CI]: -11.7% to 51.8%; P=0.15P=0.15 in HVTN 704/HPTN 085, and 8.8%; 95% CI: -45.1% to 42.6%; P=0.70P=0.70 in HVTN 703/HPTN 081).

1.2 Layered design; cause-specific risk and prevention efficacy

The AMP trials have two distinct features. First, infecting HIV-1 strains were isolated and tested for sensitivity to the study product, VRC01. HIV-1 strains are highly heterogeneous and exhibit a wide range of sensitivity to VRC01, so in addition to overall prevention efficacy, Corey et al. (2021, Figure 2) reported the prevention efficacy of the pooled VRC01 groups versus placebo against sensitive strains (estimated pooled PE = 75.4%; 95% CI: 45.5% to 88.9%), defined by an in vitro 80% inhibitory concentration IC80<1​μ\mathrm{IC}_{80}<1\,\mug/mL. Because a participant can acquire HIV-1 only once during follow-up, acquisition of a VRC01-sensitive strain and acquisition of an insensitive strain are mutually exclusive, so each is a competing event for the other.

Second, in AMP and many other efficacy trials of HIV-1 vaccines and bnAbs, all participants receive standard-of-care HIV prevention regardless of randomization arm, including facilitated access to pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), in accordance with ethics committee and institutional review board recommendations and national PrEP guidelines (Bailey and Sugarman, 2013; Gilbert et al., 2017; Gilbert, 2019; Janes et al., 2019). Daily oral PrEP effectively prevents HIV-1 acquisition, though high efficacy requires strict adherence (Baeten et al., 2012; Fonner et al., 2016; McCormack et al., 2016). We refer to such a design, in which participants in all arms receive a background intervention and an investigational intervention is added on top of this common layer, as a layered design. Primary analysis of the AMP trials compared the bnAb arm and the placebo arm as randomized; this intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis reflects the efficacy of bnAbs plus PrEP versus PrEP alone in a trial environment, where PrEP use may not reflect typical use outside the trial.

1.3 A cause-specific structural nested cumulative survival time model

Our goal is twofold. First, we estimate the causal effect of oral PrEP uptake on HIV-1 acquisition with a VRC01-sensitive strain in the AMP trials, where acquisition with a VRC01-insensitive strain is a competing event. Second, we estimate the counterfactual cumulative incidence of acquiring a VRC01-sensitive virus under a hypothetical scenario in which daily oral PrEP is withheld, or its uptake is substantially lower than observed in the AMP trial. Contrasting these counterfactual cause-specific cumulative incidence curves in the low- and high-dose arms with that in the placebo arm yields the prevention efficacy of VRC01 when daily oral PrEP is withheld, or its uptake is low. This counterfactual PE complements the original intention-to-treat analysis and helps assess the potential utility of VRC01 where PrEP uptake is low.

Structural nested cumulative survival time models (SNCSTMs) provide a principled approach to estimating the effect of a time-varying treatment process—here, oral PrEP uptake—on a time-to-event endpoint. Given an estimate of this effect, one can “blip down” the treatment process to recover the counterfactual cumulative incidence curve under a hypothetical scenario in which treatment is withheld (Robins, 2005; Seaman et al., 2020; Shi et al., 2021; Ying and Tchetgen Tchetgen, 2023; Michiels et al., 2025). Inference for these models has been developed under both sequential ignorability and instrumental variable assumptions (Seaman et al., 2020; Ying and Tchetgen Tchetgen, 2023; Michiels et al., 2025). To our knowledge, however, no variant of the SNCSTM accommodates competing events.

In this paper, we propose a cause-specific structural nested cumulative survival time model (cs-SNCSTM) and show that it relates to the Fine–Gray subdistribution hazards model in much the same way that the SNCSTM relates to Aalen’s additive hazards model. We study identification and estimation under two complementary frameworks: one based on sequential ignorability (SI) and the other based on instrumental variables (IVs). For each framework, we establish the theoretical properties of the proposed estimators of the structural parameters and evaluate their finite-sample performance through extensive simulation studies.

The SI framework suits our analysis of oral PrEP. Because participants were blinded to VRC01 assignment, PrEP uptake decisions were unlikely to depend on the randomization arm, so VRC01 assignment cannot serve as an instrument for PrEP uptake; we instead adjust for measured covariates that may affect both PrEP uptake and HIV-1 acquisition. Applying the cs-SNCSTM to HVTN 704/HPTN 085, we use SI-based methods to estimate the effect of oral PrEP on the acquisition of VRC01-sensitive and VRC01-insensitive HIV-1 strains, together with the counterfactual cause-specific cumulative incidence functions under no PrEP uptake.

The IV framework suits settings in which randomized assignment drives subsequent treatment. In the AMP trials, VRC01 infusions were administered every 8 weeks and are themselves a time-varying treatment strongly associated with the initial randomized assignment, as in the treatment-switching and time-varying compliance settings of Ying and Tchetgen Tchetgen (2023) and Michiels et al. (2025). Unlike the SI framework, the IV framework accommodates unmeasured confounding between treatment uptake and the outcome. Returning to HVTN 704/HPTN 085, we use IV-based methods to estimate the effect of VRC01 infusions on the acquisition of VRC01-sensitive and VRC01-insensitive strains, together with the cause-specific cumulative incidence functions under full adherence to the infusion schedule.

Code accompanying the paper is available via GitHub: https://github.com/Jacobs-Lee/cause-specific-SNCSTMs-simulation.

2 Models

2.1 Structural nested cumulative survival time model

We begin by reviewing the SNCSTM in the absence of competing events (Seaman et al., 2020; Shi et al., 2021; Ying and Tchetgen Tchetgen, 2023; Michiels et al., 2025). We treat the data for subjects i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n as independent and identically distributed. For each subject, let T~i\tilde{T}_{i} denote the time-to-event endpoint of interest (e.g., time to HIV-1 acquisition) and CiC_{i} the censoring time, and define the observed event time as Ti=min⁡{T~i,Ci}T_{i}=\min\{\tilde{T}_{i},C_{i}\}. The event indicator is Δi=𝟏{T~i≤Ci}\Delta_{i}=\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}_{i}\leq C_{i}\}, so that Δi=1\Delta_{i}=1 indicates the event was observed and Δi=0\Delta_{i}=0 indicates censoring. We define the counting process for the underlying event time as N~i(t)=𝟏{T~i≤t}\tilde{N}_{i}(t)=\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}_{i}\leq t\} and the observed counting process as Ni​(t)=𝟏​{Ti≤t,Δi=1}N_{i}(t)=\mathbf{1}\{T_{i}\leq t,\Delta_{i}=1\}. The associated at-risk processes are Y~i(t)=𝟏{T~i≥t}\tilde{Y}_{i}(t)=\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}_{i}\geq t\} and Yi(t)=𝟏{Ti≥t}Y_{i}(t)=\mathbf{1}\{T_{i}\geq t\}.

In addition, we assume the time-varying treatment process is measured at discrete, scheduled follow-up times 0=t1<⋯<tK+1=τ0=t_{1}<\cdots<t_{K+1}=\tau, where τ\tau denotes the end of follow-up. Let Di​(t)∈ℝD_{i}(t)\in\mathbb{R} denote the time-varying treatment uptake, and Di,k=Di​(tk)D_{i,k}=D_{i}(t_{k}) denote the treatment received at time tkt_{k}. By convention, we define Di,k=0D_{i,k}=0 if tk>T~it_{k}>\tilde{T}_{i}. We assume Di​(t)=Di,kD_{i}(t)=D_{i,k} for t∈[tk,tk+1)t\in[t_{k},t_{k+1}). The treatment uptake history up to time tkt_{k} is denoted D¯i,k={Di,l:1≤l≤k}\bar{D}_{i,k}=\{D_{i,l}:1\leq l\leq k\}, and the full treatment uptake history is denoted D¯i={Di,l:1≤l≤K}\bar{D}_{i}=\{D_{i,l}:1\leq l\leq K\}. Finally, we let ZiZ_{i} denote randomized treatment assignment at baseline and LiL_{i} denote baseline covariates, such as prognostic factors. In the treatment-switching example of Ying and Tchetgen Tchetgen (2023) and Michiels et al. (2025), ZiZ_{i} denotes the initial randomized treatment assignment and Di,kD_{i,k} the treatment actually received at time tkt_{k}. In our oral PrEP analysis of the AMP trials, ZiZ_{i} denotes the randomized bnAb assignment and Di,kD_{i,k} indicates oral PrEP uptake at time tkt_{k}. Although both examples fit within the SNCSTM framework, the relationship between ZiZ_{i} and Di,kD_{i,k} differs: in the treatment switching example, ZiZ_{i} strongly influences Di,kD_{i,k}, whereas in the oral PrEP example, ZiZ_{i} is unlikely to be associated with Di,kD_{i,k}. As discussed in Sections 3 and 4, these settings therefore call for different identification strategies and inferential methods. Throughout the remainder of the article, we drop the subscript ii when no confusion arises.

Let T~​(z,d¯k,0¯)\tilde{T}(z,\bar{d}_{k},\bar{0}) denote the potential time to the outcome had the person been assigned Z=zZ=z, with treatment uptake set to d¯k\bar{d}_{k} up to time tkt_{k} and to 00 thereafter. By the consistency assumption, T~=T~​(z,d¯k,0¯)\tilde{T}=\tilde{T}(z,\bar{d}_{k},\bar{0}) with probability one for individuals assigned Z=zZ=z whose observed treatment uptake history satisfies D¯k=d¯k\bar{D}_{k}=\bar{d}_{k} up to time tkt_{k} and equals 00 thereafter. 2.2 A cause-specific generalization of the SNCSTM and its connection to Fine–Gray subdistribution hazards model

We generalize the SNCSTM to a cause-specific version that targets a cause-specific time-to-event endpoint in the presence of competing events. Suppose there are JJ types of events, and let V∈{1,…,J}V\in\{1,\ldots,J\} denote the type of the event that occurs. Without loss of generality, we focus on the cumulative incidence of the type-11 event. In the AMP trial, for instance, there are two types of HIV-1 acquisition (J=2J=2): V=1V=1 denotes acquisition of a VRC01-sensitive strain, and V=2V=2 denotes acquisition of a VRC01-insensitive strain.

For j=1,…,Jj=1,\ldots,J, let d​N~j​(t,z,d¯)d\tilde{N}^{j}(t;z,\bar{d}) denote the increment over [t,t+dt)[t,t+dt) of the potential counting process that jumps at the time of the first event if that event is of type jj, when ZZ is set to zz and the treatment uptake process D¯\bar{D} is set to d¯\bar{d}. 3 Sequential ignorability-based methods

3.1 Identification assumptions and moment equations

The sequential ignorability-based approach treats ZZ and LL jointly as baseline covariates, denoted L∗=(Z,L)L^{*}=(Z,L). We nevertheless retain ZZ in the potential outcome notation. As discussed in Section 1.3, VRC01 assignment (ZZ) in the AMP trial is not expected to be associated with subsequent oral PrEP uptake (DkD_{k}) and therefore cannot serve as an instrument for it.

To fix ideas, we first study identification in a complete-data setting with no censoring.

Assumption 3.1 (Sequential Ignorability).

Among individuals who remain event-free at time tkt_{k}, and conditional on the treatment uptake history D¯k−1\bar{D}_{k-1} and baseline covariates L∗=(Z,L)L^{*}=(Z,L), the exposure DkD_{k} at time tkt_{k} is independent of the jump of the potential counting process for the type-1 event that would arise if all future exposures were set to zero. That is,

Dk⟂{d​N~1​(t,Z,D¯k−1,0¯):t≥tk}|D¯k−1,L∗,T~≥tk.D_{k}\perp\left\{d\tilde{N}^{1}(t;Z,\bar{D}_{k-1},\bar{0}):t\geq t_{k}\right\}\mid\bar{D}_{k-1},L^{*},\tilde{T}\geq t_{k}.

Assumption 3.1 enables us to drop DkD_{k} from the conditioning set,

\displaystyle 𝔼[dN~1(t;Z,D¯k−1,0¯)|D¯k,L∗,T~≥tk,Y~1(t;Z,D¯k−1,0¯)=1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[d\tilde{N}^{1}(t;Z,\bar{D}_{k-1},\bar{0})\;\middle|\;\bar{D}_{k},L^{*},\tilde{T}\geq t_{k},\tilde{Y}^{1}(t;Z,\bar{D}_{k-1},\bar{0})=1\right] (3.1)
=\displaystyle={} 𝔼[dN~1(t;Z,D¯k−1,0¯)|D¯k−1,L∗,T~≥tk,Y~1(t;Z,D¯k−1,0¯)=1].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[d\tilde{N}^{1}(t;Z,\bar{D}_{k-1},\bar{0})\;\middle|\;\bar{D}_{k-1},L^{*},\tilde{T}\geq t_{k},\tilde{Y}^{1}(t;Z,\bar{D}_{k-1},\bar{0})=1\right].

Combining Equation (3.1) with Equation (2.5), we obtain the following core equation

𝔼[\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigl[ 𝟏{T~≥tk}(Dk−𝔼[Dk∣D¯k−1,L∗,T~≥tk,Y~1(t;Z,D¯k,0¯)=1])\displaystyle\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}\geq t_{k}\}\left(D_{k}-\mathbb{E}[D_{k}\mid\bar{D}_{k-1},L^{*},\tilde{T}\geq t_{k},\tilde{Y}^{1}(t;Z,\bar{D}_{k},\bar{0})=1]\right) (3.3)
×Y~1(t)(dN~1(t)−DkdBD(t))]=0,\displaystyle\times\tilde{Y}^{1}(t)\left(d\tilde{N}^{1}(t)-D_{k}dB_{D}(t)\right)\Bigr]=0,

which we prove formally in Supplementary Material A.1.1. However, estimating BD​(t)B_{D}(t) from the moment equation (3.3) faces two impediments. First, the conditioning event in the nuisance function 𝔼[Dk∣D¯k−1,L∗,T~≥tk,Y~1(t;Z,D¯k,0¯)=1]\mathbb{E}\left[D_{k}\mid\bar{D}_{k-1},L^{*},\tilde{T}\geq t_{k},\tilde{Y}^{1}(t;Z,\bar{D}_{k},\bar{0})=1\right] involves the potential outcome Y~1​(t,Z,D¯k,0¯)\tilde{Y}^{1}(t;Z,\bar{D}_{k},\bar{0}). Second, quantities such as Y~1​(t)\tilde{Y}^{1}(t) and N~1​(t)\tilde{N}^{1}(t) are not always observable in the presence of censoring. We address these two impediments in turn.

First, for t∈[tk,tk+1)t\in[t_{k},t_{k+1}), we define the interval-wise cumulative effect Ak​(t)=∫tktd​BD​(s)A_{k}(t)=\int_{t_{k}}^{t}dB_{D}(s) and the following treatment residual:

ek​(t∣D¯k−1,L∗,T≥tk)=Dk−𝔼[Dkexp{−DkAk(t−)}|D¯k−1,L∗,T≥tk]𝔼[exp{−DkAk(t−)}|D¯k−1,L∗,T≥tk],e_{k}(t\mid\bar{D}_{k-1},L^{*},T\geq t_{k})=D_{k}-\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[D_{k}\exp\left\{-D_{k}A_{k}(t^{-})\right\}\Bigm|\bar{D}_{k-1},L^{*},T\geq t_{k}\right]}{\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left\{-D_{k}A_{k}(t^{-})\right\}\Bigm|\bar{D}_{k-1},L^{*},T\geq t_{k}\right]},

which depends only on the observed-data distribution. Proposition 3.1 shows that the residual Dk−𝔼[Dk∣D¯k−1,L∗,T~≥tk,Y~1(t;D¯k,0¯)=1]D_{k}-\mathbb{E}\left[D_{k}\mid\bar{D}_{k-1},L^{*},\widetilde{T}\geq t_{k},\widetilde{Y}^{1}(t;\bar{D}_{k},\bar{0})=1\right] appearing in the moment equation (3.3) equals ek​(t∣D¯k−1,L∗,T≥tk)e_{k}(t\mid\bar{D}_{k-1},L^{*},T\geq t_{k}), and is therefore identified from the observed data.

Proposition 3.1.

Suppose that the cause-specific SNCSTM (2.4), and Assumptions 2.1 and 3.1 hold. For k=1,…,Kk=1,\ldots,K and t∈[tk,tk+1)t\in[t_{k},t_{k+1}), we have

Dk−𝔼[Dk∣D¯k−1,L∗,T~≥tk,Y~1(t;D¯k,0¯)=1]=ek(t∣D¯k−1,L∗,T≥tk).D_{k}-\mathbb{E}\left[D_{k}\mid\bar{D}_{k-1},L^{*},\widetilde{T}\geq t_{k},\widetilde{Y}^{1}(t;\bar{D}_{k},\bar{0})=1\right]=e_{k}(t\mid\bar{D}_{k-1},L^{*},T\geq t_{k}). (3.4)

Second, let CC be the censoring time and assume conditional independent censoring, as formalized in Assumption 3.2.

Assumption 3.2 (Conditional independent censoring).
C⟂({dN~j(t):t∈[0,τ],j=1,⋯,J},D¯K)∣L∗C\perp(\{d\tilde{N}^{j}(t):t\in[0,\tau],j=1,\cdots,J\},\bar{D}_{K})\mid L^{*}

Assumption 3.2 requires the censoring time variable CC to be independent of the event processes and the full treatment history, conditional on the baseline covariates L∗L^{*}. For t∈[0,τ]t\in[0,\tau], define

r(t)=𝟏{C≥T~∧t},G(t∣L∗)=P(C≥t∣L∗),r(t)=\mathbf{1}\{C\geq\tilde{T}\wedge t\},\qquad G(t\mid L^{*})=P(C\geq t\mid L^{*}),
w⁡(t)=r⁡(t)​G​(t∣L∗)G⁡(T∧t∣L∗),Y1,w​(t)=w⁡(t)​Y1​(t),w(t)=\frac{r(t)G(t\mid L^{*})}{G(T\wedge t\mid L^{*})},\qquad Y^{1,w}(t)=w(t)Y^{1}(t),

so that Y1,w​(t)Y^{1,w}(t) is always observable, and

Yˇ1(t)=𝟏{T≥tk}Y1,w(t),t∈[tk,tk+1).\check{Y}^{1}(t)=\mathbf{1}\{T\geq t_{k}\}Y^{1,w}(t),\quad t\in[t_{k},t_{k+1}).

Theorem 3.1 adapts inverse probability of censoring weighting (IPCW) to construct a valid moment equation under covariate-dependent censoring.

Theorem 3.1 (Moment equation in the presence of censoring).

Suppose that the cause-specific SNCSTM (2.4), and Assumptions 2.1–3.2 hold. Assume further that G⁡(t∣L∗)>0G(t\mid L^{*})>0 for all t∈[0,τ]t\in[0,\tau] and LL. Then, for each k=1,…,Kk=1,\ldots,K and all t∈[tk,tk+1)t\in[t_{k},t_{k+1}),

𝔼⁡[ek​(t∣D¯k−1,L∗,T≥tk)​Yˇ1​(t)​(d​N1​(t)−Dk​d​BD​(t))]=0.\mathbb{E}\left[{e_{k}(t\mid\bar{D}_{k-1},L^{*},T\geq t_{k})}\check{Y}^{1}(t)\left(dN^{1}(t)-D_{k}\,dB_{D}(t)\right)\right]=0. (3.5)

We will refer to (3.5) as the SI moment equation. Equation (3.5) involves only observed quantities. Constructing an estimating equation from it requires estimating two nuisance functions: the conditional survival function G⁡(t∣L∗)G(t\mid L^{\ast}) of the censoring time, and the conditional distribution of DkD_{k} given the observed history among those with T≥tkT\geq t_{k}.

3.2 Estimation and inference for parameters in cause-specific SNCSTMs

Proposition 3.2.

For t∈[tk,tk+1)t\in[t_{k},t_{k+1}), assume that BD​(t)B_{D}(t) is continuous. Under Assumptions 2.1–3.2, and the cause-specific SNCSTM (2.4), the parameter of interest Ak​(t)A_{k}(t) that solves the SI moment equation (3.5) admits the following closed-form solution

Ak​(t)=∫tkt𝔼⁡[ek​(s∣D¯k−1,L∗,T≥tk)​d​N1​(s)]𝔼⁡[ek​(s∣D¯k−1,L∗,T≥tk)​Yˇ1​(s)​Dk],A_{k}(t)=\int_{t_{k}}^{t}\frac{\mathbb{E}[e_{k}(s\mid\bar{D}_{k-1},L^{*},T\geq t_{k})dN^{1}(s)]}{\mathbb{E}[e_{k}(s\mid\bar{D}_{k-1},L^{*},T\geq t_{k})\check{Y}^{1}(s)D_{k}]},

We order the cause-1 event times s1<⋯<sMs_{1}<\cdots<s_{M}, where {s1,⋯,sM}={Ti:Δi=1,Vi=1}\{s_{1},\cdots,s_{M}\}=\{T_{i}:\Delta_{i}=1,V_{i}=1\}. Also define Δ​Ni1​(sm)=𝟏​{Ti=sm,Δi=1,Vi=1}\Delta N^{1}_{i}(s_{m})=\mathbf{1}\{T_{i}=s_{m},\Delta_{i}=1,V_{i}=1\}. A^k​(t)=∑tk≤sm≤td​A^k​(sm)=∑tk≤sm≤t∑i=1nei,k​(sm,θ^)​Δ​Ni1​(sm)∑i=1nei,k​(sm,θ^)​Yˇi1​(sm,θ^)​Di,k,\hat{A}_{k}(t)=\sum_{t_{k}\leq s_{m}\leq t}d\hat{A}_{k}(s_{m})=\sum_{t_{k}\leq s_{m}\leq t}\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}e_{i,k}(s_{m};\hat{\theta})\Delta N_{i}^{1}(s_{m})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}e_{i,k}(s_{m};\hat{\theta})\check{Y}^{1}_{i}(s_{m};\hat{\theta})D_{i,k}},

B^D​(t)=∑j=1kA^j​(t∧tj+1−).\hat{B}_{D}(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{k}\hat{A}_{j}(t\wedge t_{j+1}^{-}).

Propositions 3.3 and 3.4 establish the theoretical properties of B^D​(t)\hat{B}_{D}(t).

Proposition 3.3.

Under the regularity conditions in Supplemental Material A.1.3, the estimator B^D​(t)\hat{B}_{D}(t) is uniformly consistent for BD​(t)B_{D}(t); that is,

supt∈[0,τ]|B^D​(t)−BD​(t)|→𝑃0as ​n→∞.\sup_{t\in[0,\tau]}|\hat{B}_{D}(t)-B_{D}(t)|\xrightarrow{P}0\quad\text{as }n\to\infty.

1n​∑i=1nψ^i2​(t,θ^),\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{\psi}_{i}^{2}(t;\hat{\theta}),

where ψ^i​(t,θ^)\hat{\psi}_{i}(t;\hat{\theta}) is defined in Supplemental Material A.1.4.

If one further assumes a constant-effect model, that is, BD​(t)=β​tB_{D}(t)=\beta t, then β\beta can be estimated by (see, e.g., Ying and Tchetgen Tchetgen, 2023)

If tk+1−tkt_{k+1}-t_{k} is constant for every k=1,…,Kk=1,\ldots,K, then the periodic effect Ak​(t)≡A​(t)A_{k}(t)\equiv A(t) can be estimated by

A^​(t)=∫0t∑k=1KW~​(tk+s)​d​B^D​(tk+s)∑k=1KW~​(tk+s).\hat{A}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{K}\tilde{W}(t_{k}+s)d\hat{B}_{D}(t_{k}+s)}{\sum_{k=1}^{K}\tilde{W}(t_{k}+s)}.

4 Instrumental variable-based methods

4.1 Identification assumptions and moment equations

In applications where the time-varying treatment process D¯\bar{D} denotes time-varying adherence to the randomized treatment assignment ZZ, one may instead leverage the fact that ZZ is a valid instrumental variable to identify the structural parameters in Equation (2.4), analogous to the identification of structural parameters in SNCSTMs in the absence of competing events (Ying and Tchetgen Tchetgen, 2023; Michiels et al., 2025).

We assume that ZZ satisfies the standard instrumental variable assumptions formalized in Assumptions 4.1–4.3.

Assumption 4.1 (IV relevance).
Z⟂̸Dk|D¯k−1,L,T~≥tkZ\not\perp D_{k}\mid\bar{D}_{k-1},L,\tilde{T}\geq t_{k}

Assumption 4.1 requires that the instrument ZZ be associated with the treatment received at time tkt_{k}, conditional on the observed treatment history, baseline covariates, and survival to tkt_{k}. This assumption may fail when DkD_{k} represents a subsequent treatment decision that is not directly influenced by ZZ. For instance, in the AMP trial, assignment to VRC01 versus placebo is unlikely to be associated with a participant’s oral PrEP uptake, since the trial is blinded. By contrast, the IV relevance assumption typically holds when DkD_{k} represents adherence to the treatment assigned by ZZ. In the AMP trial, VRC01 infusions were administered every 88 weeks, so if DkD_{k} denotes the kk-th infusion, the initial randomization ZZ serves as an instrument for DkD_{k}.

Assumption 4.2 (Exclusion restriction).

For any fixed treatment history d¯\bar{d}, the instrumental variable ZZ has no direct effect on the potential counting process of any event type. That is, for any z,z′z,z^{\prime} and j∈{1,…,J}j\in\{1,\ldots,J\},

d​N~j​(t,z,d¯)=d​N~j​(t,z′,d¯),∀t∈[0,τ].d\tilde{N}^{j}(t;z,\bar{d})=d\tilde{N}^{j}(t;z^{\prime},\bar{d}),\quad\forall t\in[0,\tau].

Assumption 4.2 requires that ZZ affect the potential counting processes only through the treatment uptake process, with no direct effect once the treatment history is fixed. We can therefore write d​N~j​(t,z,d¯)d\tilde{N}^{j}(t;z,\bar{d}) as d​N~j​(t,d¯)d\tilde{N}^{j}(t;\bar{d}). Assumption 4.2 is most plausible in a blinded trial, where participants are unaware of their treatment assignment.

Assumption 4.3 (IV independence).
Z⟂{dN~j(t;0¯):t∈[0,τ],j=1,⋯,J}∣LZ\perp\{d\tilde{N}^{j}(t;\bar{0}):t\in[0,\tau],j=1,\cdots,J\}\mid L

Assumption 4.3 states that, conditional on LL, ZZ is independent of the potential counting process for any event type under no treatment uptake. This assumption holds by design in randomized trials.

Remark 4.1 (Role of unmeasured confounders).

Unmeasured confounding of the relationship between treatment received and the outcome violates sequential ignorability but is permitted under the IV framework, provided the instrumental variable assumptions hold. The IV approach is therefore a useful alternative when sequential ignorability is implausible.

We next impose the conditional independent censoring assumption.

Assumption 4.4 (Conditional independent censoring).
C⟂({dN~j(t):t∈[0,τ],j=1,⋯,J},D¯K,Z)∣LC\perp(\{d\tilde{N}^{j}(t):t\in[0,\tau],j=1,\cdots,J\},\bar{D}_{K},Z)\mid L

Theorem 4.1 establishes an IV moment equation under Assumptions 4.1–4.4.

Theorem 4.1 (IV moment equation).

Suppose that the cause-specific SNCSTM (2.4), Assumptions 2.1 and  4.1–4.4 hold. Assume further that G⁡(t∣L)>0G(t\mid L)>0 for all t∈(0,τ]t\in(0,\tau] and LL. Then for t∈[0,τ]t\in[0,\tau], the following moment condition holds:

𝔼⁡[(Z−𝔼⁡[Z∣L])​Yˇ1​(t)​exp⁡{∫0t−D⁡(s)​d​BD​(s)}​(d​N1​(t)−D⁡(t)​d​BD​(t))]=0.\mathbb{E}\left[\left(Z-\mathbb{E}[Z\mid L]\right)\check{Y}^{1}(t)\exp\left\{\int_{0}^{t^{-}}D(s)\,dB_{D}(s)\right\}\left(dN^{1}(t)-D(t)\,dB_{D}(t)\right)\right]=0. (4.1)

We will refer to (4.1) as the IV moment equation.

4.2 Estimation and inference for parameters in cause-specific SNCSTMs

Proposition 4.1 gives a closed-form expression for BD​(t)B_{D}(t) that solves the IV moment equation.

Proposition 4.1.

Write Zc=Z−𝔼⁡[Z∣L]Z^{c}=Z-\mathbb{E}[Z\mid L], and assume that BD​(t)B_{D}(t) is continuous in tt. Under the cause-specific SNCSTM (2.4) and Assumptions 2.1 and 4.1–4.4, the parameter of interest BD​(t)B_{D}(t) that solves the IV moment equation (4.1) admits the following closed-form solution

BD​(t)=∫0t𝔼⁡[Zc​exp⁡{∫0s−D⁡(u)​d​BD​(u)}​d​N1​(s)]𝔼⁡[Zc​Yˇ1​(s)​exp⁡{∫0s−D⁡(u)​d​BD​(u)}​D​(s)],B_{D}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[Z^{c}\exp\{\int_{0}^{s^{-}}D(u)dB_{D}(u)\}dN^{1}(s)\right]}{\mathbb{E}\left[Z^{c}\check{Y}^{1}(s)\exp\{\int_{0}^{s^{-}}D(u)dB_{D}(u)\}D(s)\right]}, (4.2)

provided that 𝔼⁡[Zc​Yˇ1​(t)​exp⁡{∫0t−D⁡(s)​d​BD​(s)}​D​(t)]≠0\mathbb{E}\left[Z^{c}\check{Y}^{1}(t)\exp\{\int_{0}^{t^{-}}D(s)dB_{D}(s)\}D(t)\right]\neq 0 for all t∈(0,τ]t\in(0,\tau].

Let θ\theta denote parameters indexing the treatment assignment model 𝔼[Z∣L;θ]\mathbb{E}[Z\mid L;\theta] and the censoring model G⁡(t∣L;θ)G(t\mid L;\theta), and let θ^\hat{\theta} denote a consistent and asymptotically linear estimator of θ\theta. Let s1<⋯<sMs_{1}<\cdots<s_{M} and Δ​Ni1​(sm)\Delta N^{1}_{i}(s_{m}) be defined the same as in Section 3.2. An estimator B^D​(t)\hat{B}_{D}(t) for BD​(t)B_{D}(t) can be obtained using the following recursive form:

B^D​(t)=∑sm≤td​B^D​(sm)=∑sm≤t∑iZic​(θ^)​exp⁡{∑1≤l<mDi​(sl)​d​B^D​(sl)}​Δ​Ni1​(sm)∑iZic​(θ^)​Yˇi1​(sm,θ^)​exp⁡{∑1≤l<mDi​(sl)​d​B^D​(sl)}​Di​(sm),\hat{B}_{D}(t)=\sum_{s_{m}\leq t}d\hat{B}_{D}(s_{m})=\sum_{s_{m}\leq t}\frac{\sum_{i}Z_{i}^{c}(\hat{\theta})\exp\left\{\sum_{1\leq l<m}D_{i}(s_{l})d\hat{B}_{D}(s_{l})\right\}\Delta N_{i}^{1}(s_{m})}{\sum_{i}Z_{i}^{c}(\hat{\theta})\check{Y}^{1}_{i}(s_{m};\hat{\theta})\exp\left\{\sum_{1\leq l<m}D_{i}(s_{l})d\hat{B}_{D}(s_{l})\right\}D_{i}(s_{m})}, (4.3)

with initial value B^D​(0)=0\hat{B}_{D}(0)=0.

Finally, Propositions 4.2 and 4.3 establish the properties of B^D​(t)\hat{B}_{D}(t).

Proposition 4.2.

Under the regularity conditions in Supplemental Material A.2.2, the estimator B^D​(t)\hat{B}_{D}(t) is uniformly consistent for BD​(t)B_{D}(t); that is,

supt∈[0,τ]|B^D​(t)−BD​(t)|→𝑃0as ​n→∞.\sup_{t\in[0,\tau]}|\hat{B}_{D}(t)-B_{D}(t)|\xrightarrow{P}0\quad\text{as }n\to\infty. (4.4)
Proposition 4.3.

Under conditions in Supplemental Material A.2.3, the normalized process n​{B^D​(t)−BD​(t)}\sqrt{n}\{\hat{B}_{D}(t)-B_{D}(t)\} converges weakly to a mean-zero Gaussian process with variance function that can be consistently estimated by

1n​∑i=1nϵ^i2​(t,θ^),\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{\epsilon}_{i}^{2}(t;\hat{\theta}), (4.5)

where ϵ^i2​(t,θ^)\hat{\epsilon}_{i}^{2}(t;\hat{\theta}) is defined in Supplemental Material A.2.3.

5 Counterfactual cause-specific cumulative incidence function

With the estimated treatment effect, B^D​(t)\hat{B}_{D}(t), we can blip down the observed treatment uptake D¯\bar{D} to 0¯\bar{0}, yielding the counterfactual cause-specific cumulative incidence that would have been observed in the absence of any treatment uptake. Theorem 5.1 derives the expected value of the subdistribution risk indicator for the type-11 event under treatment assignment Z=zZ=z and no treatment uptake.

Theorem 5.1.

Suppose that the cause-specific SNCSTM (2.4), and the assumptions underpinning Theorem 3.1 or 4.1 hold (where we replace LL with L∗L^{*} in the following under sequential ignorability). Then, for each k=1,…,Kk=1,\ldots,K and all t∈[tk,tk+1)t\in[t_{k},t_{k+1}),

𝔼​[Y~1​(t,Z,0¯)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\tilde{Y}^{1}(t;Z,\bar{0})\Bigr] =𝔼[∑j=1k−1𝟏{tj≤T<tj+1,Δ=1,V≠1}exp⁡{∫0t∧tj+1D⁡(s)​d​BD​(s)}G⁡(T∣L)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Biggl[\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\mathbf{1}\{t_{j}\leq T<t_{j+1},\,\Delta=1,\,V\neq 1\}\frac{\exp\{\int_{0}^{t\wedge t_{j+1}}D(s)dB_{D}(s)\}}{G(T\mid L)} (5.1)
+𝟏{T≥tk}Y1,w​(t)​exp⁡{∫0t∧tk+1D⁡(s)​d​BD​(s)}G⁡(t∣L)].\displaystyle+\mathbf{1}\{T\geq t_{k}\}\frac{Y^{1,w}(t)\exp\{\int_{0}^{t\wedge t_{k+1}}D(s)dB_{D}(s)\}}{G(t\mid L)}\Biggr].

In particular, only the second term in Equation (5.1) remains if t∈[0,t2)t\in[0,t_{2}). The counterfactual cause-1-specific cumulative incidence under the treatment assignment ZZ in the absence of time-varying treatment uptake is

F1​(t):=P⁡{T~​(Z,0¯)≤t,V⁡(Z,0¯)=1}=1−𝔼⁡[Y~1​(t,Z,0¯)],F^{1}(t):=P\{\tilde{T}(Z,\bar{0})\leq t,V(Z,\bar{0})=1\}=1-\mathbb{E}[\tilde{Y}^{1}(t;Z,\bar{0})], (5.2)

which can be estimated by plugging in fitted nuisance models and estimated BD​(⋅)B_{D}(\cdot). Following Propositions 3.4 and 4.3, if the estimated parameter θ^\hat{\theta} in nuisance functions is regular and asymptotically linear, then the plug-in estimator of F1​(t)F^{1}(t) is also regular and asymptotically linear. Nonparametric bootstrap can then be used to obtain confidence intervals for each fixed tt.

6 Simulation

Our goal is to evaluate the finite-sample performance of the proposed estimators for BD​(t)B_{D}(t) in cause-specific SNCSTMs under both sequential ignorability-based and instrumental variable-based frameworks. In all settings, we consider three treatment uptake intervals, [t1,t2)[t_{1},t_{2}), [t2,t3)[t_{2},t_{3}), and [t3,t4)[t_{3},t_{4}), with (t1,t2,t3,t4)=(0,0.5,1,1.5)(t_{1},t_{2},t_{3},t_{4})=(0,0.5,1,1.5) and administrative follow-up ending at τ=t4\tau=t_{4}. We consider three values of sample size nn: 10001000, 50005000, and 1000010000.

We generate baseline covariates differently in the SI and IV settings:

SI settings

We independently generate two observed baseline covariates: L1∼N⁡(0,1)L_{1}\sim N(0,1) truncated to [−3,3][-3,3] and L2∼Bernoulli⁡(0.5)L_{2}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(0.5). Using the notation in Section 3, L∗=(L1,L2)L^{\ast}=(L_{1},L_{2}).

IV settings

In addition to L1L_{1} and L2L_{2} generated as in the SI settings, we generate an unmeasured baseline covariate UU with P⁡(U=−1)=P⁡(U=1)=1/2P(U=-1)=P(U=1)=1/2, and a randomized three-level instrument Z∈{0,1,2}Z\in\{0,1,2\} with P⁡(Z=z)=1/3P(Z=z)=1/3 for z=0,1,2z=0,1,2. Both UU and ZZ are independent of each other and of (L1,L2)(L_{1},L_{2}).

Next, we generate the treatment uptake (D1,D2,D3)(D_{1},D_{2},D_{3}) in the SI and IV settings as follows:

SI settings

We let logit⁡P⁡(D1=1∣L)=−1+0.3​L1+0.3​(L2−0.5),\operatorname{logit}P(D_{1}=1\mid L)=-1+0.3L_{1}+0.3(L_{2}-0.5), and, for k=2,3k=2,3,

logit⁡P⁡(Dk=1∣D¯k−1,L)=−1.7+2​Dk−1+0.6​D~k−1+0.3​L1+0.3​(L2−0.5),\operatorname{logit}P(D_{k}=1\mid\bar{D}_{k-1},L)=-1.7+2D_{k-1}+0.6\,\widetilde{D}_{k-1}+0.3L_{1}+0.3(L_{2}-0.5),

where D~k−1=(k−1)−1​∑s=1k−1Ds\widetilde{D}_{k-1}=(k-1)^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^{k-1}D_{s} is the average of past treatment uptake. This data generating process satisfies sequential ignorability.

IV settings

We let logit⁡P⁡(D1=1∣L,U,Z)=−1+0.3​L1+0.3​(L2−0.5)+0.8​Z+0.3​U,\operatorname{logit}P(D_{1}=1\mid L,U,Z)=-1+0.3L_{1}+0.3(L_{2}-0.5)+0.8Z+0.3U, and, for k=2,3k=2,3,

logit⁡P⁡(Dk=1∣D¯k−1,L,U,Z)=\displaystyle\operatorname{logit}P(D_{k}=1\mid\bar{D}_{k-1},L,U,Z)={} −1.7+2​Dk−1+0.6​D~k−1\displaystyle-1.7+2D_{k-1}+0.6\,\widetilde{D}_{k-1}
+0.3​L1+0.3​(L2−0.5)+0.8​Z+0.3​U.\displaystyle+0.3L_{1}+0.3(L_{2}-0.5)+0.8Z+0.3U.

For notational convenience, let XX denote the full set of baseline variables in the potential-outcome model: X=(L1,L2)X=(L_{1},L_{2}) in the SI setting and X=(L1,L2,U)X=(L_{1},L_{2},U) in the IV setting. By the exclusion restriction, ZZ has no direct effect on the outcome, so XX does not include ZZ. We specify the following cause-specific cumulative incidence functions when there is no treatment uptake (i.e., D¯=0¯\bar{D}=\bar{0}) as

F1​(t;0¯∣X)=0.6​m​(X)​H0.025​(t),F2​(t;0¯∣X)=0.4​m​(X)​H0.035​(t),F_{1}(t;\bar{0}\mid X)=0.6m(X)H_{0.025}(t),\hskip 18.49988ptF_{2}(t;\bar{0}\mid X)=0.4m(X)H_{0.035}(t),

where, for 0≤t≤τ0\leq t\leq\tau, Ha​(t)=1−e−a​t1−e−a​τH_{a}(t)=\frac{1-e^{-at}}{1-e^{-a\tau}}, m⁡(X)=expit⁡{b+η⁡(X)}m(X)=\operatorname{expit}\{b+\eta(X)\}, and

We consider four overall event probabilities by the end of follow-up under D¯=0¯\bar{D}=\bar{0} and in the absence of censoring, r∈{7%,15%,30%,60%}r\in\{7\%,15\%,30\%,60\%\}, and calibrate the parameter bb separately in the SI and IV settings to achieve each target.

Write Fj(t;d¯k,0¯∣X)=P{T~(d¯k,0¯)≤t,V(d¯k,0¯)=j∣X},k=0,1,2,3.F_{j}(t;\bar{d}_{k},\bar{0}\mid X)=P\left\{\tilde{T}(\bar{d}_{k},\bar{0})\leq t,\,V(\bar{d}_{k},\bar{0})=j\mid X\right\},~k=0,1,2,3. We consider the following cause-jj-specific SNCSTM:

P⁡(Y~j​(t,Z,D¯k,0¯)=1∣D¯k,Z,L,T~≥tk)P⁡(Y~j​(t,Z,D¯k−1,0¯)=1∣D¯k,Z,L,T~≥tk)=exp⁡{−βj(k)​Dk​(min⁡(t,tk+1)−tk)}\frac{P(\tilde{Y}^{j}(t;Z,\bar{D}_{k},\bar{0})=1\mid\bar{D}_{k},Z,L,\tilde{T}\geq t_{k})}{P(\tilde{Y}^{j}(t;Z,\bar{D}_{k-1},\bar{0})=1\mid\bar{D}_{k},Z,L,\tilde{T}\geq t_{k})}=\exp\left\{-\beta^{(k)}_{j}D_{k}\bigl(\min(t,t_{k+1})-t_{k}\bigr)\right\}

and a time-homogeneous setting in which β1(1)=β1(2)=β1(3)=β1=−0.25​r\beta_{1}^{(1)}=\beta_{1}^{(2)}=\beta_{1}^{(3)}=\beta_{1}=-0.25r and β2(1)=β2(2)=β2(3)=β2=−0.125​r\beta_{2}^{(1)}=\beta_{2}^{(2)}=\beta_{2}^{(3)}=\beta_{2}=-0.125r. As shown in the Supplemental Material B.1, Fj​(t;d¯k,0¯∣X)F_{j}(t;\bar{d}_{k},\bar{0}\mid X) satisfies the following recursive relationship:

Fj​(t;d¯k,0¯∣X)\displaystyle F_{j}(t;\bar{d}_{k},\bar{0}\mid X) =Fj​(t;d¯k−1,0¯∣X)+\displaystyle={}F_{j}(t;\bar{d}_{k-1},\bar{0}\mid X)+
{1−F3−j​(tk;d¯k−1,0¯∣X)−Fj​(t;d¯k−1,0¯∣X)}×[1−exp⁡{−βj​dk​(min⁡(t,tk+1)−tk)}],\displaystyle\left\{1-F_{3-j}(t_{k};\bar{d}_{k-1},\bar{0}\mid X)-F_{j}(t;\bar{d}_{k-1},\bar{0}\mid X)\right\}\times\left[1-\exp\left\{-\beta_{j}d_{k}\bigl(\min(t,t_{k+1})-t_{k}\bigr)\right\}\right],

for tk≤t≤τt_{k}\leq t\leq\tau, while Fj​(t;d¯k,0¯∣X)=Fj​(t;d¯k−1,0¯∣X)F_{j}(t;\bar{d}_{k},\bar{0}\mid X)=F_{j}(t;\bar{d}_{k-1},\bar{0}\mid X) for t<tkt<t_{k}. Hence, starting from Fj​(t;0¯∣X)F_{j}(t;\bar{0}\mid X), we apply this recursive relationship sequentially to obtain the cause-specific cumulative incidence under each treatment uptake trajectory d¯k\bar{d}_{k}.

Finally, latent censoring time C∗C^{*} is generated independently of the event process and treatment assignments conditional on LL, using a Cox proportional hazards model with hazard

hC​(t∣L1,L2)=2​λC​0​t​exp⁡{0.3​L1+0.3​(L2−0.5)}.h_{C}(t\mid L_{1},L_{2})=2\lambda_{C0}t\exp\left\{0.3L_{1}+0.3(L_{2}-0.5)\right\}.

We set λC​0=0.045\lambda_{C0}=0.045 so that P⁡(C∗<τ)≈0.10P(C^{*}<\tau)\approx 0.10 and let C=min⁡(C∗,τ)C=\min(C^{*},\tau).

In both the SI and IV settings, for each data-generating process (specified by the sample size nn and event rate rr) and each cause jj, we computed (i) the proposed nonparametric estimator B^D​(t)\hat{B}_{D}(t) of BD​(t)B_{D}(t), evaluated at t∈{t2,t3,t4}t\in\{t_{2},t_{3},t_{4}\}, and (ii) the averaged estimator β^\hat{\beta} of β\beta. For each estimator, we report the absolute relative bias, Monte Carlo standard deviation (MCSD), mean estimated standard error (SE), and coverage percentage (CP) of the 95% confidence interval. Results are based on 10,000 simulation replications per setting.

Table 1 summarizes the simulation results for an event rate of 30%. Under both the SI and IV settings, the relative bias was small across all sample sizes, remaining below 1% in most cases and decreasing as the sample size increased. The mean estimated standard errors closely matched the Monte Carlo standard deviations, and the empirical coverage of the 95% confidence intervals was close to the nominal level. Results for other event rates, reported in Section B.2 of the Supplementary Material, are qualitatively similar to those in Table 1.

7 HVTN 704/HPTN 085

7.1 Effect of oral PrEP and “oral PrEP-free” cause-specific CIFs

We first study the causal effect of oral PrEP on HIV-1 acquisition with a VRC01-sensitive strain and with a VRC01-insensitive strain, as well as the counterfactual cumulative incidence of each in the absence of oral PrEP.

In the AMP trials, oral PrEP use was quantified using two biomarkers measured in dried blood spots (DBS): emtricitabine triphosphate (FTC-TP) and tenofovir diphosphate (TFV-DP), the intracellular active metabolites of emtricitabine and tenofovir, respectively, the two components of oral PrEP. Both were measured in all cases and in a subset of non-cases selected by sampling stratified by VRC01 arm and self-reported oral PrEP uptake. The resulting longitudinal DBS cohort comprised 174 participants (54 cases and 120 non-cases), whose biomarkers were measured at study visits approximately every 8 weeks. FTC-TP has a half-life of approximately 35 hours in DBS, whereas TFV-DP has a half-life of approximately 17 days (Castillo-Mancilla et al., 2013). Because TFV-DP may accumulate over weeks, TFV-DP detected during a period [tk,tk+1)[t_{k},t_{k+1}) may partly reflect oral PrEP use in earlier periods. FTC-TP, by contrast, mainly reflects recent use (Castillo-Mancilla et al., 2013; Anderson et al., 2018), so we used FTC-TP in our analysis.

We consider K=10K=10 time intervals and administrative censoring at τ=560\tau=560 days (corresponding to 88 weeks post the last scheduled infusion), with [tk,tk+1)=[56​(k−1),56​k)[t_{k},t_{k+1})=[56(k-1),56k) for k=1,…,9k=1,\ldots,9 and [t10,τ]=[504,560][t_{10},\tau]=[504,560]. Within each interval [tk,tk+1)[t_{k},t_{k+1}), we let Dk=1D_{k}=1 if the first FTC-TP measurement between [tk,tk+1)[t_{k},t_{k+1}) was at or above the lower limit of quantification (LLOQ), and Dk=0D_{k}=0 otherwise; a detectable FTC-TP level indicates recent use of daily oral PrEP. The primary outcome of interest is HIV-1 acquisition with a VRC01-sensitive strain, defined as a strain with IC80≤3​μ​g/mL\mathrm{IC}_{80}\leq 3\,\mu\mathrm{g/mL}, and the competing event is HIV-1 acquisition with a VRC01-insensitive strain, defined as a strain with IC80>3​μ​g/mL\mathrm{IC}_{80}>3\,\mu\mathrm{g/mL}.

We estimated BD​(t)B_{D}(t) in the cause-specific SNCSTM under the sequential ignorability assumption. When constructing the estimator, we fitted the conditional censoring distribution using Cox regression adjusting for age, and the propensity score gk=f⁡(Dk∣D¯k−1,L∗,T~≥tk)g_{k}=f(D_{k}\mid\bar{D}_{k-1},L^{*},\tilde{T}\geq t_{k}) using logistic regression adjusting for age and average oral PrEP uptake up to time tkt_{k}.

Figure 1 shows B^D​(t)\hat{B}_{D}(t), the estimated cumulative effect of oral PrEP on acquisition of VRC01-sensitive (left panel) and VRC01-insensitive (right panel) HIV-1 strains, with shaded bands indicating 95% pointwise confidence intervals. Here, B^D​(t)\hat{B}_{D}(t) is the cumulative effect through time tt on the subdistribution hazard scale. For example, B^D​(t)=−0.01\hat{B}_{D}(t)=-0.01 corresponds roughly to one fewer HIV-1 acquisition of the given strain type per 100 participants who would remain free of that strain type by time tt under continuous oral PrEP use through tt, compared with no use. For both strain types, the estimates become progressively more negative over follow-up, suggesting a protective effect of oral PrEP (Grant et al., 2010, see, e.g.,).

If we further assume a constant additive effect on the subdistribution hazard, that is, BD​(t)=β​tB_{D}(t)=\beta t, the estimated effect of oral PrEP is −1.49×10−5-1.49\times 10^{-5} per day (95% CI: −3.38×10−5-3.38\times 10^{-5} to 0.41×10−50.41\times 10^{-5}) on the acquisition of VRC01-sensitive strains and −4.00×10−5-4.00\times 10^{-5} per day (95% CI: −5.84×10−5-5.84\times 10^{-5} to −2.16×10−5-2.16\times 10^{-5}) on the acquisition of VRC01-insensitive strains. Both estimates are negative, but only the 95% confidence interval for VRC01-insensitive strains excludes zero.

Finally, Figure 2 compares two sets of strain-specific CIFs, both pooled across the VRC01 arms: the estimated counterfactual CIFs under no oral PrEP uptake (orange solid lines), and the intention-to-treat CIFs estimated from a Fine–Gray model, which reflect oral PrEP uptake as it actually occurred (black dashed lines). For both causes, the “oral PrEP-free” cumulative incidences are higher than the observed ones, again consistent with a protective effect of oral PrEP.

To assess the robustness of our findings, we conducted a sensitivity analysis where we defined D1D_{1} using the FTC-TP measurement on day 0 and DkD_{k} using the last FTC-TP measurement in (tk−1,tk](t_{k-1},t_{k}] for k≥2k\geq 2, rather than the first measurement between [tk,tk+1)[t_{k},t_{k+1}). The result, reported in Supplementary Material C, is qualitatively similar to those presented above.

7.2 Effect of VRC01 infusion and a per-protocol reanalysis

We next studied the effect of VRC01 infusions administered every 8 weeks at 10 mg/kg or 30 mg/kg on the acquisition of VRC01-sensitive and VRC01-insensitive HIV-1 strains, as well as the counterfactual cause-specific cumulative incidence functions under full adherence to the VRC01 infusion schedule. After excluding participants with missing primary outcome data, unknown strain sensitivity, or no follow-up, the analysis included 2,642 participants who had been randomized in a 1:1:1 ratio to high-dose VRC01 at 30 mg/kg (Z=2Z=2), low-dose VRC01 at 10 mg/kg (Z=1Z=1), or placebo (Z=0Z=0).

We estimated the effect of each VRC01 dose separately, comparing participants randomized to that dose (30 mg/kg or 10 mg/kg) with those randomized to placebo. We used the same K=10K=10 time intervals with administrative censoring at τ=560\tau=560 days as in the previous analysis. These 10 intervals correspond to the 10 scheduled infusions. For each interval, we defined Dk=1D_{k}=1 if the participant received placebo or skipped the scheduled infusion, and Dk=0D_{k}=0 if the participant received the scheduled VRC01 infusion. Because only participants randomized to a VRC01 arm could receive VRC01, randomized assignment is a strong instrumental variable for subsequent VRC01 infusions.

Figure 3 shows the estimated cumulative effects, obtained using the IV-based methods described in Section 4.2, of omitting versus receiving VRC01 infusions every 8 weeks at 10 mg/kg (top panels) and 30 mg/kg (bottom panels). For both doses, omitting VRC01 appeared to increase the risk of acquiring VRC01-sensitive, but not VRC01-insensitive, HIV-1 strains.

If we further assume a constant additive effect on the hazard, that is, BD​(t)=β​tB_{D}(t)=\beta t, the estimated effects of omitting 10 mg/kg VRC01 infusions are 1.79×10−51.79\times 10^{-5} per day (95% CI: −0.51×10−5-0.51\times 10^{-5} to 4.08×10−54.08\times 10^{-5}) on the acquisition of VRC01-sensitive strains and −0.57×10−5-0.57\times 10^{-5} per day (95% CI: −3.30×10−5-3.30\times 10^{-5} to 2.15×10−52.15\times 10^{-5}) on the acquisition of VRC01-insensitive strains. The corresponding estimates for the 30 mg/kg dose are 2.09×10−52.09\times 10^{-5} per day (95% CI: −0.18×10−5-0.18\times 10^{-5} to 4.36×10−54.36\times 10^{-5}) and −0.54×10−5-0.54\times 10^{-5} per day (95% CI: −3.29×10−5-3.29\times 10^{-5} to 2.22×10−52.22\times 10^{-5}), respectively. Although all confidence intervals include zero, the estimates for VRC01-sensitive strains point toward increased risk without VRC01 at both doses, whereas those for VRC01-insensitive strains are close to zero. These findings are consistent with the expectation that the protective effect of VRC01 depends on the sensitivity of the infecting strain to the antibody (Wu et al., 2010; Corey et al., 2021).

Finally, Figure 4 shows the estimated cause-specific CIFs under a counterfactual scenario in which participants received all scheduled VRC01 infusions (“per-protocol”), alongside the intention-to-treat estimates. For both doses and both causes, the per-protocol estimates were close to the intention-to-treat estimates, consistent with the high adherence to the infusion schedule in the trial: participants received a mean of 9.0 infusions, and 79% received all 10.

8 Discussion

We generalized the structural nested cumulative survival time model to a cause-specific version and studied estimation and inference under two complementary frameworks: sequential ignorability (SI) and instrumental variables (IV). The IV framework is suited to settings in which the randomized treatment assignment is associated with subsequent treatment uptake, for example, when uptake represents adherence to the assigned treatment. The SI framework applies when no such instrument is available, for example when uptake involves a treatment not influenced by the initial assignment, provided that all confounders of uptake and the outcome are measured.

We applied both methods to HVTN 704/HPTN 085, one of the two Antibody Mediated Prevention (AMP) trials. In the first part of the case study, we estimated that oral PrEP uptake reduced the risk of HIV-1 acquisition for both VRC01-sensitive and VRC01-insensitive strains, consistent with oral PrEP’s mechanism of HIV-1 prevention. Using the proposed method, we also recovered the cause-specific cumulative incidence functions in the absence of oral PrEP uptake. In the second part, we found that VRC01 infusions administered every 8 weeks tended to reduce the risk of acquiring VRC01-sensitive strains, with no apparent effect on VRC01-insensitive strains. This pattern agrees with the sieve analysis reported by Corey et al. (2021). The proposed method also provides a principled way to estimate the per-protocol effect, that is, the effect under full adherence to the scheduled VRC01 infusions.

The proposed methods can also be applied to the other AMP trial, HVTN 703/HPTN 081. However, we did not pursue this analysis because oral PrEP uptake was very low among women participants in sub-Saharan Africa in HVTN 703/HPTN 081. During 3300 person-years of follow-up in HVTN 703/HPTN 081, oral PrEP was detectable in only 3.8% (95% CI: 2.8 to 4.9) person-years (Corey et al., 2021).

The oral PrEP analysis was constrained by the granularity of the available data. Because the oral PrEP biomarkers were measured approximately every 8 weeks, we used 8-week time intervals and treated oral PrEP uptake as constant within each interval. With more frequent measurements of oral PrEP use, the analysis could be adapted to a finer time grid, under which the assumption of constant uptake within intervals would be more plausible.

Appendix A Proofs

We provide more detailed proofs of uniform consistency and weak convergence for the IV-based strategy. The corresponding proofs under sequential ignorability follow similar arguments, so we omit repetitive steps.

A.1 Sequential ignorability-based Strategy

A.1.1 Proof of Theorem 3.1

Proof.

In the following proof, we make no distinction between LL and L∗L^{*}, and omit ZZ in the potential outcome for simplicity.

For data without censoring, we establish the validity of its moment equation first.

Lemma A.1.

Under the cause-specific SNCSTM (2.4), consistency, and Assumption 3.1, for each k=1,…,Kk=1,\ldots,K and all t∈[tk,tk+1)t\in[t_{k},t_{k+1}),

𝔼[𝟏{T~≥tk}(Dk−𝔼[Dk∣D¯k−1,L,T~≥tk,Y~1(t;D¯k,0¯)=1])Y~1(t)(dN~1(t)−DkdBD(t))]=0.\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}\geq t_{k}\}\Bigl(D_{k}-\mathbb{E}[D_{k}\mid\bar{D}_{k-1},L,\tilde{T}\geq t_{k},\tilde{Y}^{1}(t;\bar{D}_{k},\bar{0})=1]\Bigr)\tilde{Y}^{1}(t)\Bigl(d\tilde{N}^{1}(t)-D_{k}\,dB_{D}(t)\Bigr)\Bigr]=0. For incomplete data, where Y1,c​(t)Y^{1,c}(t) is unobservable, we need IPCW weights in Fine and Gray (1999) to construct observable indicator Y1,w​(t)Y^{1,w}(t). Use 𝒪t\mathcal{O}_{t} to denote observed history up to tt. An important property of this weight is

𝔼⁡[Y1,c​(t)∣𝒪t]=Y1,w​(t)\mathbb{E}[Y^{1,c}(t)\mid\mathcal{O}_{t}]=Y^{1,w}(t)

Prove this first. Consider 4 cases. If 𝒪t\mathcal{O}_{t} indicates {T≥t}\{T\geq t\}, then Y1,c​(t)=1Y^{1,c}(t)=1. If 𝒪t\mathcal{O}_{t} indicates {T<t,Δ=1,V=1}\{T<t,\Delta=1,V=1\} or {T<t,Δ=0}\{T<t,\Delta=0\}, then Y1,c​(t)=0Y^{1,c}(t)=0. If 𝒪t\mathcal{O}_{t} indicates {T<t,Δ=1,V≠1}\{T<t,\Delta=1,V\neq 1\}, then

𝔼⁡[Y1,c​(t)∣𝒪t]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[Y^{1,c}(t)\mid\mathcal{O}_{t}] =𝔼[𝟏{C≥t}∣𝒪t]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}\{C\geq t\}\mid\mathcal{O}_{t}]
=P⁡(C≥t∣C≥T,L)\displaystyle=P(C\geq t\mid C\geq T,L)
=G⁡(t∣L)G⁡(T∣L)\displaystyle=\frac{G(t\mid L)}{G(T\mid L)}

This proves the stated property. So, within the expectation, Y1,w​(t)Y^{1,w}(t) can be viewed as Y1,c​(t)Y^{1,c}(t). Then we are able to establish the validity of the moment equation.

A.1.4 Proof of Proposition 3.4

We aim to provide a sum of i.i.d representation of n​(A^k​(t)−Ak​(t))\sqrt{n}(\hat{A}_{k}(t)-A_{k}(t)) heuristically. =\displaystyle= 𝔼[exp{𝒜1(t)}(𝔼[𝟏{T~<t2,V≠1}+𝔼[Y~1(t;D¯1,0¯)∣H1,T~≥t2]𝟏{T~≥t2}∣H1])∣L]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\exp\{\mathcal{A}_{1}(t)\}\Bigl(\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}<t_{2},V\neq 1\}+\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\tilde{Y}^{1}(t;\bar{D}_{1},\bar{0})\mid H_{1},\tilde{T}\geq t_{2}\Bigr]\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}\geq t_{2}\}\mid H_{1}\Bigr]\Bigr)\mid L\Bigr]
=\displaystyle= 𝔼[exp{𝒜1(t)}(𝔼[𝟏{T~<t2,V≠1}+𝔼[𝔼[Y~1(t;D¯1,0¯)∣H2]∣H1,T~≥t2]𝟏{T~≥t2}∣H1])∣L]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\exp\{\mathcal{A}_{1}(t)\}\Bigl(\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}<t_{2},V\neq 1\}+\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\mathbb{E}[\tilde{Y}^{1}(t;\bar{D}_{1},\bar{0})\mid H_{2}]\mid H_{1},\tilde{T}\geq t_{2}\Bigr]\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}\geq t_{2}\}\mid H_{1}\Bigr]\Bigr)\mid L\Bigr]
=\displaystyle= 𝔼[exp{𝒜1(t)}(𝔼[𝟏{T~<t2,V≠1}+𝔼[exp{𝒜2(t)}𝔼[Y~1(t;D¯2,0¯)∣H2]∣H1,T~≥t2]𝟏{T~≥t2}∣H1])∣L]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\exp\{\mathcal{A}_{1}(t)\}\Bigl(\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}<t_{2},V\neq 1\}+\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\exp\{\mathcal{A}_{2}(t)\}\mathbb{E}[\tilde{Y}^{1}(t;\bar{D}_{2},\bar{0})\mid H_{2}]\mid H_{1},\tilde{T}\geq t_{2}\Bigr]\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}\geq t_{2}\}\mid H_{1}\Bigr]\Bigr)\mid L\Bigr]
=\displaystyle= 𝔼[exp{𝒜1(t)}(𝔼[𝟏{T~<t2,V≠1}+𝔼[exp{𝒜2(t)}Y~1(t;D¯2,0¯)∣H1,T~≥t2]𝟏{T~≥t2}∣H1])∣L]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\exp\{\mathcal{A}_{1}(t)\}\Bigl(\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}<t_{2},V\neq 1\}+\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\exp\{\mathcal{A}_{2}(t)\}\tilde{Y}^{1}(t;\bar{D}_{2},\bar{0})\mid H_{1},\tilde{T}\geq t_{2}\Bigr]\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}\geq t_{2}\}\mid H_{1}\Bigr]\Bigr)\mid L\Bigr]
=\displaystyle= 𝔼[exp{𝒜1(t)}𝟏{T~<t2,V≠1}+𝔼[𝔼[exp{𝒜1(t)+𝒜2(t)}Y~1(t;D¯2,0¯)∣H1,T~≥t2]𝟏{T~≥t2}∣H1]∣L]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\exp\{\mathcal{A}_{1}(t)\}\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}<t_{2},V\neq 1\}+\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\exp\{\mathcal{A}_{1}(t)+\mathcal{A}_{2}(t)\}\tilde{Y}^{1}(t;\bar{D}_{2},\bar{0})\mid H_{1},\tilde{T}\geq t_{2}\Bigr]\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}\geq t_{2}\}\mid H_{1}\Bigr]\mid L\Bigr]
=\displaystyle= 𝔼[exp{𝒜1(t)}𝟏{T~<t2,V≠1}+exp{Γ2(t)}Y~1(t)𝟏{T~≥t2}∣L]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\exp\{\mathcal{A}_{1}(t)\}\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}<t_{2},V\neq 1\}+\exp\{\Gamma_{2}(t)\}\tilde{Y}^{1}(t)\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}\geq t_{2}\}\mid L\Bigr]

The final equality is because

𝔼[𝔼[exp{Γ2(t)}Y~1(t;D¯2,0¯)∣H1,𝟏{T~≥t2}=1]𝟏{T~≥t2}∣H1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\mathbb{E}[\exp\{\Gamma_{2}(t)\}\tilde{Y}^{1}(t;\bar{D}_{2},\bar{0})\mid H_{1},\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}\geq t_{2}\}=1]\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}\geq t_{2}\}\mid H_{1}\Bigr]
=\displaystyle= 𝔼[𝔼[exp{Γ2(t)}Y~1(t;D¯2,0¯)∣H1,𝟏{T~≥t2}]𝟏{T~≥t2}∣H1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\mathbb{E}[\exp\{\Gamma_{2}(t)\}\tilde{Y}^{1}(t;\bar{D}_{2},\bar{0})\mid H_{1},\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}\geq t_{2}\}]\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}\geq t_{2}\}\mid H_{1}\Bigr]
=\displaystyle= 𝔼[exp{Γ2(t)}Y~1(t;D¯2,0¯)𝟏{T~≥t2}∣H1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\exp\{\Gamma_{2}(t)\}\tilde{Y}^{1}(t;\bar{D}_{2},\bar{0})\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}\geq t_{2}\}\mid H_{1}\Bigr]

So iteratively, we can prove that for t∈[tk,tk+1)t\in[t_{k},t_{k+1}), there exists

𝔼​[Y~1​(t,0¯)∣L]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\tilde{Y}^{1}(t;\bar{0})\mid L\Bigr]
=\displaystyle= {𝔼⁡[Y~1​(t)​exp⁡{Γ1​(t)}∣L],k=1,𝔼[∑j=1k−1𝟏{tj≤T~<tj+1,V≠1}exp{Γj(t)}+𝟏{T~≥tk}Y~1(t)exp{Γk(t)}∣L],k≥2.\displaystyle\begin{cases}\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\tilde{Y}^{1}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{1}(t)\}\mid L\Bigr],&k=1,\\[10.00002pt] \mathbb{E}\Bigl[\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\mathbf{1}\{t_{j}\leq\tilde{T}<t_{j+1},V\neq 1\}\exp\{\Gamma_{j}(t)\}+\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}\geq t_{k}\}\tilde{Y}^{1}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{k}(t)\}\mid L\Bigr],&k\geq 2.\end{cases}

This proves the lemma.

For data without censoring, we can directly use this result to obtain

P⁡(T~​(0¯)≤t,V⁡(0¯)=1∣L)=1−𝔼⁡[Y~1​(t,0¯)∣L]P(\tilde{T}(\bar{0})\leq t,V(\bar{0})=1\mid L)=1-\mathbb{E}[\tilde{Y}^{1}(t;\bar{0})\mid L] (A.4)
Step 2

Consider censoring CC and observed survival time T=min⁡{T~,C}T=\min\{\tilde{T},C\}. We can observe

N1​(t)\displaystyle N^{1}(t) :=𝟏​{T≤t,Δ=1,V=1}\displaystyle:=\mathbf{1}\{T\leq t,\Delta=1,V=1\}
Y1​(t)\displaystyle Y^{1}(t) :=𝟏{T≥t}+𝟏{T<t,Δ=1,V≠1}\displaystyle:=\mathbf{1}\{T\geq t\}+\mathbf{1}\{T<t,\Delta=1,V\neq 1\}

Define Y1,c(t)=𝟏{C≥t}Y~1(t)Y^{1,c}(t)=\mathbf{1}\{C\geq t\}\tilde{Y}^{1}(t). Consider Y1,c​(t)Y^{1,c}(t) observable first, like in censoring-complete data, Y1​(t)=Y1,c​(t)Y^{1}(t)=Y^{1,c}(t). For k=1k=1, we have

𝔼⁡[Y1,c​(t)​exp⁡{Γ1​(t)}∣L]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigl[Y^{1,c}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{1}(t)\}\mid L\Bigr] =𝔼[𝟏{C≥t}Y~1(t)exp{Γ1(t)}∣L]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\mathbf{1}\{C\geq t\}\tilde{Y}^{1}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{1}(t)\}\mid L\Bigr]
=P⁡(C≥t∣L)​𝔼​[Y~1​(t)​exp⁡{Γ1​(t)}∣L]\displaystyle=P(C\geq t\mid L)\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\tilde{Y}^{1}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{1}(t)\}\mid L\Bigr]

So 𝔼⁡[Y~1​(t)​exp⁡{Γ1​(t)}∣L]=𝔼⁡[Y1,c​(t)​exp⁡{Γ1​(t)}∣L]P⁡(C≥t∣L)\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\tilde{Y}^{1}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{1}(t)\}\mid L\Bigr]=\frac{\mathbb{E}\Bigl[Y^{1,c}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{1}(t)\}\mid L\Bigr]}{P(C\geq t\mid L)}

For k≥2k\geq 2, let us focus on the right term first.

𝔼[𝟏{T≥tk}Y1,c(t)exp{Γk(t)}∣L]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\mathbf{1}\{T\geq t_{k}\}Y^{1,c}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{k}(t)\}\mid L\Bigr] =𝔼[𝟏{C≥tk}𝟏{T~≥tk}𝟏{C≥t}Y~1(t)exp{Γk(t)}∣L]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\mathbf{1}\{C\geq t_{k}\}\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}\geq t_{k}\}\mathbf{1}\{C\geq t\}\tilde{Y}^{1}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{k}(t)\}\mid L\Bigr]
=𝔼[𝟏{C≥t}𝟏{T~≥tk}Y~1(t)exp{Γk(t)}∣L]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\mathbf{1}\{C\geq t\}\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}\geq t_{k}\}\tilde{Y}^{1}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{k}(t)\}\mid L\Bigr]
=P(C≥t∣L)𝔼[𝟏{T~≥tk}Y~1(t)exp{Γk(t)}∣L]\displaystyle=P(C\geq t\mid L)\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}\geq t_{k}\}\tilde{Y}^{1}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{k}(t)\}\mid L\Bigr]

So we can use the observed variables to do expectations.

𝔼[𝟏{T~≥tk}Y~1(t)exp{Γk(t)}∣L]=𝔼[𝟏{T≥tk}Y1,c(t)exp{Γk(t)}∣L]P⁡(C≥t∣L)\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}\geq t_{k}\}\tilde{Y}^{1}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{k}(t)\}\mid L\Bigr]=\frac{\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\mathbf{1}\{T\geq t_{k}\}Y^{1,c}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{k}(t)\}\mid L\Bigr]}{P(C\geq t\mid L)}

For the left term, we have

𝔼[∑j=1k−1𝟏{tj≤T<tj+1,Δ=1,V≠1}1G⁡(T∣L)exp{Γj(t)}∣L]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\mathbf{1}\{t_{j}\leq T<t_{j+1},\Delta=1,V\neq 1\}\frac{1}{G(T\mid L)}\exp\{\Gamma_{j}(t)\}\mid L\Bigr]
=\displaystyle= ∑j=1k−1𝔼[𝟏{tj≤T~<tj+1,V≠1}𝟏{C≥T~}G⁡(T∣L)exp{Γj(t)}∣L]\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\mathbf{1}\{t_{j}\leq\tilde{T}<t_{j+1},V\neq 1\}\frac{\mathbf{1}\{C\geq\tilde{T}\}}{G(T\mid L)}\exp\{\Gamma_{j}(t)\}\mid L\Bigr]
=\displaystyle= ∑j=1k−1𝔼[𝟏{tj≤T~<tj+1,V≠1}𝔼[𝟏{C≥T~}∣T~,V,D¯,L]G⁡(T~∣L)exp{Γj(t)}∣L]\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\mathbf{1}\{t_{j}\leq\tilde{T}<t_{j+1},V\neq 1\}\frac{\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}\{C\geq\tilde{T}\}\mid\tilde{T},V,\bar{D},L]}{G(\tilde{T}\mid L)}\exp\{\Gamma_{j}(t)\}\mid L\Bigr]
=\displaystyle= ∑j=1k−1𝔼[𝟏{tj≤T~<tj+1,V≠1}exp{Γj(t)}∣L]\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\mathbf{1}\{t_{j}\leq\tilde{T}<t_{j+1},V\neq 1\}\exp\{\Gamma_{j}(t)\}\mid L\Bigr]

As a result, we can use observed variables to blip down and calculate the expectation.

𝔼​[Y~1​(t,0¯)∣L]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\tilde{Y}^{1}(t;\bar{0})\mid L\Bigr] (A.5)
=\displaystyle= {𝔼⁡[Y1,c​(t)​exp⁡{Γ1​(t)}G⁡(t∣L)∣L],k=1,𝔼[∑j=1k−1𝟏{tj≤T<tj+1,Δ=1,V≠1}exp⁡{Γj​(t)}G⁡(T∣L)+𝟏{T≥tk}Y1,c​(t)​exp⁡{Γk​(t)}G⁡(t∣L)∣L],k≥2.\displaystyle\begin{cases}\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\frac{Y^{1,c}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{1}(t)\}}{G(t\mid L)}\mid L\Bigr],&k=1,\\[10.00002pt] \mathbb{E}\Bigl[\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\mathbf{1}\{t_{j}\leq T<t_{j+1},\Delta=1,V\neq 1\}\frac{\exp\{\Gamma_{j}(t)\}}{G(T\mid L)}\\ \qquad\qquad+\mathbf{1}\{T\geq t_{k}\}\frac{Y^{1,c}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{k}(t)\}}{G(t\mid L)}\mid L\Bigr],&k\geq 2.\end{cases}

Recall that for incomplete-censoring data, Y1,w​(t)Y^{1,w}(t) can replace unobservable Y1,c​(t)Y^{1,c}(t) within expectations. So this equation becomes

𝔼​[Y~1​(t,0¯)∣L]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\tilde{Y}^{1}(t;\bar{0})\mid L\Bigr] (A.6)
=\displaystyle= {𝔼⁡[Y1,w​(t)​exp⁡{Γ1​(t)}G⁡(t∣L)∣L],k=1,𝔼[∑j=1k−1𝟏{tj≤T<tj+1,Δ=1,V≠1}exp⁡{Γj​(t)}G⁡(T∣L)+𝟏{T≥tk}Y1,w​(t)​exp⁡{Γk​(t)}G⁡(t∣L)∣L],k≥2.\displaystyle\begin{cases}\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\frac{Y^{1,w}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{1}(t)\}}{G(t\mid L)}\mid L\Bigr],&k=1,\\[10.00002pt] \mathbb{E}\Bigl[\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\mathbf{1}\{t_{j}\leq T<t_{j+1},\Delta=1,V\neq 1\}\frac{\exp\{\Gamma_{j}(t)\}}{G(T\mid L)}\\ \qquad\qquad+\mathbf{1}\{T\geq t_{k}\}\frac{Y^{1,w}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{k}(t)\}}{G(t\mid L)}\mid L\Bigr],&k\geq 2.\end{cases}

Finally, marginalizing over LL yields the desired result.

A.2 IV-based Strategy

A.2.1 Proof of Theorem 4.1

We view ZZ as a baseline covariate first. According to Lemma A.4, there exists

𝔼[Y~1(t;0¯)∣Z,L]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\tilde{Y}^{1}(t;\bar{0})\mid Z,L\Bigr] (A.7)
=\displaystyle= {𝔼[Y~1(t)exp{Γ1(t)}∣Z,L],k=1,𝔼[∑j=1k−1𝟏{tj≤T~<tj+1,V≠1}exp{Γj(t)}+𝟏{T~≥tk}Y~1(t)exp{Γk(t)}∣Z,L],k≥2.\displaystyle\begin{cases}\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\tilde{Y}^{1}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{1}(t)\}\mid Z,L\Bigr],&k=1,\\[10.00002pt] \mathbb{E}\Bigl[\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\mathbf{1}\{t_{j}\leq\tilde{T}<t_{j+1},V\neq 1\}\exp\{\Gamma_{j}(t)\}+\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}\geq t_{k}\}\tilde{Y}^{1}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{k}(t)\}\mid Z,L\Bigr],&k\geq 2.\end{cases}

Define the subdistribution hazard function as follows.

λ01​(t∣L):=\displaystyle\lambda_{0}^{1}(t\mid L):= dd​t​P​(T~​(0¯)≤t,V⁡(0¯)=1∣L)1−P⁡(T~​(0¯)≤t,V⁡(0¯)=1∣L)\displaystyle\frac{\frac{d}{dt}P(\tilde{T}{(\bar{0})}\leq t,V(\bar{0})=1\mid L)}{1-P(\tilde{T}{(\bar{0})}\leq t,V(\bar{0})=1\mid L)}
=\displaystyle= dd​tP(T~(0¯)≤t,V(0¯)=1∣Z,L)1−P(T~(0¯)≤t,V(0¯)=1∣Z,L)\displaystyle\frac{\frac{d}{dt}P(\tilde{T}{(\bar{0})}\leq t,V(\bar{0})=1\mid Z,L)}{1-P(\tilde{T}{(\bar{0})}\leq t,V(\bar{0})=1\mid Z,L)}
=\displaystyle= −dd​tlog(1−P(T~(0¯)≤t,V(0¯)=1∣Z,L))\displaystyle-\frac{d}{dt}\log(1-P(\tilde{T}(\bar{0})\leq t,V(\bar{0})=1\mid Z,L))
=\displaystyle= −dd​tlog(𝔼[Y~1(t;0¯)∣Z,L])\displaystyle-\frac{d}{dt}\log(\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\tilde{Y}^{1}(t;\bar{0})\mid Z,L\Bigr])

The first equality is due to IV independence. Then based on (A.7), we keep on calculating. For simplicity, define

Qk(t)=∑j=1k−1𝟏{tj≤T~<tj+1,V≠1}exp{Γj(t)}+𝟏{T~≥tk}Y~1(t)exp{Γk(t)}.Q_{k}(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\mathbf{1}\{t_{j}\leq\tilde{T}<t_{j+1},V\neq 1\}\exp\{\Gamma_{j}(t)\}+\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}\geq t_{k}\}\tilde{Y}^{1}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{k}(t)\}.

Then we have

λ01​(t∣L)\displaystyle\lambda_{0}^{1}(t\mid L) =−dd​tlog(𝔼[Qk(t)∣Z,L])\displaystyle=-\frac{d}{dt}\log\Bigl(\mathbb{E}\Bigl[Q_{k}(t)\mid Z,L\Bigr]\Bigr)
λ01(t∣L)𝔼[Qk(t)∣Z,L]dt\displaystyle\lambda_{0}^{1}(t\mid L)\mathbb{E}\Bigl[Q_{k}(t)\mid Z,L\Bigr]dt =−d𝔼[Qk(t)∣Z,L]\displaystyle=-d\mathbb{E}\Bigl[Q_{k}(t)\mid Z,L\Bigr]

Now focus on d𝔼[Qk(t)∣Z,L]d\mathbb{E}[Q_{k}(t)\mid Z,L]. For t∈[tk,tk+1)t\in[t_{k},t_{k+1}), the first part of Qk​(t)Q_{k}(t) is fixed. So we only need to differentiate on the second part. So the right term is

d𝔼[Qk(t)∣Z,L]\displaystyle d\mathbb{E}\Bigl[Q_{k}(t)\mid Z,L\Bigr]
=\displaystyle= 𝔼[d(𝟏{T~≥tk}Y~1(t)exp{Γk(t)})∣Z,L]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigl[d\Bigl(\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}\geq t_{k}\}\tilde{Y}^{1}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{k}(t)\}\Bigr)\mid Z,L\Bigr]
=\displaystyle= 𝔼[𝟏{T~≥tk}(dY~1(t)exp{Γk(t)}+Y~1(t)dd​texp{Γk(t)}dt)∣Z,L]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}\geq t_{k}\}\Bigl(d\tilde{Y}^{1}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{k}(t)\}+\tilde{Y}^{1}(t)\frac{d}{dt}\exp\{\Gamma_{k}(t)\}dt\Bigr)\mid Z,L\Bigr]
=\displaystyle= 𝔼[𝟏{T~≥tk}(−dN~1(t)exp{Γk(t)}+Y~1(t)exp{Γk(t)}DkdBD(t))∣Z,L]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}\geq t_{k}\}\Bigl(-d\tilde{N}^{1}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{k}(t)\}+\tilde{Y}^{1}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{k}(t)\}D_{k}dB_{D}(t)\Bigr)\mid Z,L\Bigr]

The left term is

λ01(t∣L)𝔼[Qk(t)∣Z,L]dt\displaystyle\lambda_{0}^{1}(t\mid L)\mathbb{E}\Bigl[Q_{k}(t)\mid Z,L\Bigr]dt =λ01(t∣L)𝔼[Y~1(t;0¯)∣Z,L]dt\displaystyle=\lambda_{0}^{1}(t\mid L)\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\tilde{Y}^{1}(t;\bar{0})\mid Z,L\Bigr]dt
=λ01​(t∣L)​𝔼​[Y~1​(t,0¯)∣L]​d​t\displaystyle=\lambda_{0}^{1}(t\mid L)\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\tilde{Y}^{1}(t;\bar{0})\mid L\Bigr]dt

Rearranging yields

𝔼[𝟏{T~≥tk}Y~1(t)exp{Γk(t)}{dN~1(t)−DkdBD(t)}−𝔼[Y~1(t;0¯)∣L]λ01(t∣L)dt|Z,L]=0\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}\geq t_{k}\}\tilde{Y}^{1}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{k}(t)\}\Bigl\{d\tilde{N}^{1}(t)-D_{k}dB_{D}(t)\Bigr\}-\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\tilde{Y}^{1}(t;\bar{0})\mid L\Bigr]\lambda_{0}^{1}(t\mid L)dt\;\Bigm|\;Z,L\Bigg]=0 (A.8)

Add the residual term Z−𝔼⁡[Z∣L]Z-\mathbb{E}[Z\mid L] in the above equation, then we get

𝔼[(Z−𝔼[Z∣L])𝟏{T~≥tk}Y~1(t)exp{Γk(t)}(dN~1(t)−DkdBD(t))∣L]=0.\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\Bigl(Z-\mathbb{E}[Z\mid L]\Bigr)\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}\geq t_{k}\}\tilde{Y}^{1}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{k}(t)\}\Bigl(d\tilde{N}^{1}(t)-D_{k}dB_{D}(t)\Bigr)\mid L\Bigg]=0. (A.9)

For data without censoring, this can be the moment equation. Consider censoring CC. We assume Y1,c(t)=𝟏{C≥t}Y~1(t)Y^{1,c}(t)=\mathbf{1}\{C\geq t\}\tilde{Y}^{1}(t) can be observed first, like censoring-complete data. Consider the following equation.

𝔼[(Z−𝔼[Z∣L])𝟏{T≥tk}Y1,c(t)exp{Γk(t)}(dN1(t)−DkdBD(t))∣L]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\Bigl(Z-\mathbb{E}[Z\mid L]\Bigr)\mathbf{1}\{T\geq t_{k}\}Y^{1,c}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{k}(t)\}\Bigl(dN^{1}(t)-D_{k}dB_{D}(t)\Bigr)\mid L\Bigg]
=\displaystyle= 𝔼[(Z−𝔼[Z∣L])𝟏{T~≥tk}𝟏{C≥tk}𝟏{C≥t}Y~1(t)exp{Γk(t)}𝟏{C≥t}(dN~1(t)−DkdBD(t))∣L]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\Bigl(Z-\mathbb{E}[Z\mid L]\Bigr)\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}\geq t_{k}\}\mathbf{1}\{C\geq t_{k}\}\mathbf{1}\{C\geq t\}\tilde{Y}^{1}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{k}(t)\}\mathbf{1}\{C\geq t\}\Bigl(d\tilde{N}^{1}(t)-D_{k}dB_{D}(t)\Bigr)\mid L\Bigg]
=\displaystyle= 𝔼[(Z−𝔼[Z∣L])𝟏{T~≥tk}𝟏{C≥t}Y~1(t)exp{Γk(t)}(dN~1(t)−DkdBD(t))∣L]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\Bigl(Z-\mathbb{E}[Z\mid L]\Bigr)\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}\geq t_{k}\}\mathbf{1}\{C\geq t\}\tilde{Y}^{1}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{k}(t)\}\Bigl(d\tilde{N}^{1}(t)-D_{k}dB_{D}(t)\Bigr)\mid L\Bigg]
=\displaystyle= P(C≥t∣L)𝔼[(Z−𝔼[Z∣L])𝟏{T~≥tk}Y~1(t)exp{Γk(t)}(dN~1(t)−DkdBD(t))∣L]\displaystyle P(C\geq t\mid L)\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\Bigl(Z-\mathbb{E}[Z\mid L]\Bigr)\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{T}\geq t_{k}\}\tilde{Y}^{1}(t)\exp\{\Gamma_{k}(t)\}\Bigl(d\tilde{N}^{1}(t)-D_{k}dB_{D}(t)\Bigr)\mid L\Bigg]
=\displaystyle= 0\displaystyle 0

So this is a valid moment equation. For incomplete-censoring data, as we discussed before, observable Y1,wY^{1,w} can replace unobservable Y1,c​(t)Y^{1,c}(t) within expectations. So the moment equation turns out to be

A.2.2 Proof of Proposition 4.2

Appendix B Additional details on the simulation studies

B.1 Recursive rules for CIFs

We imposed the stronger joint ignorability condition

D¯K⟂{(T~​(d¯),V⁡(d¯)):d¯∈{0,1}K}|X.\bar{D}_{K}\perp\left\{\bigl(\tilde{T}(\bar{d}),V(\bar{d})\bigr):\bar{d}\in\{0,1\}^{K}\right\}\mid X.

Thus, the conditioning on the observed treatment history in the SNCSTM can be removed. For cause jj, the structural model implies, for t≥tkt\geq t_{k},

1−P{T~(d¯k,0¯)≤t,V(d¯k,0¯)=j∣T~(d¯k,0¯)≥tk,X}1−P{T~(d¯k−1,0¯)≤t,V(d¯k−1,0¯)=j∣T~(d¯k−1,0¯)≥tk,X}=exp⁡{−βj​dk​(min⁡(t,tk+1)−tk)}.\frac{1-P\left\{\tilde{T}(\bar{d}_{k},\bar{0})\leq t,V(\bar{d}_{k},\bar{0})=j\mid\tilde{T}(\bar{d}_{k},\bar{0})\geq t_{k},X\right\}}{1-P\left\{\tilde{T}(\bar{d}_{k-1},\bar{0})\leq t,V(\bar{d}_{k-1},\bar{0})=j\mid\tilde{T}(\bar{d}_{k-1},\bar{0})\geq t_{k},X\right\}}=\exp\left\{-\beta_{j}d_{k}\bigl(\min(t,t_{k+1})-t_{k}\bigr)\right\}.

B.2 Simulation Results

Tables 2, 3, and 4 summarize the simulation results for event rates of 7%7\%, 15%15\%, and 60%60\%, respectively. Across these scenarios, both the SI and IV settings exhibited generally modest absolute relative biases. Mean estimated standard errors closely matched the Monte Carlo standard deviations, and empirical coverage remained near the nominal 95% level, with mild undercoverage in some scenarios. Monte Carlo standard deviations decreased as the sample size increased, indicating improved precision.

Appendix C Sensitivity analysis for the case study

In a sensitivity analysis, we use the last FTC-TP measurement within each interval [tk,tk+1)[t_{k},t_{k+1}) and define Dk=1D_{k}=1 if it exceeds the LLOQ of 0.1​pmol/sample0.1\,\mathrm{pmol/sample}, and Dk=0D_{k}=0 otherwise. In a second sensitivity analysis, we define D1D_{1} using the FTC-TP measurement on day 0 and, for k≥2k\geq 2, define DkD_{k} using the last FTC-TP measurement in (tk−1,tk](t_{k-1},t_{k}]. All other analysis settings remain the same. Figure 5 shows B^D​(t)\hat{B}_{D}(t), the estimated cumulative effect of oral PrEP on the acquisition of VRC01-sensitive (left panel) and VRC01-insensitive (right panel) HIV-1 strains, with shaded bands indicating 95% pointwise confidence intervals. If we further assume a constant additive effect on the subdistribution hazard, that is, BD​(t)=β​tB_{D}(t)=\beta t, the estimated effect of oral PrEP is −3.41×10−5-3.41\times 10^{-5} per day (95% CI: −6.57×10−5-6.57\times 10^{-5} to −0.24×10−5-0.24\times 10^{-5}) on the acquisition of VRC01-sensitive strains and −3.44×10−5-3.44\times 10^{-5} per day (95% CI: −5.36×10−5-5.36\times 10^{-5} to −1.52×10−5-1.52\times 10^{-5}) on the acquisition of VRC01-insensitive strains. Both estimates are negative and their confidence intervals do not contain zero. Figure 6 shows the estimated “blipped-down” cause-specific CIFs under no oral PrEP uptake, pooled across the VRC01 arms, alongside the observed cause-specific CIFs estimated from the Fine–Gray model without removing the effect of oral PrEP uptake. For both causes, the “oral PrEP-free” cumulative incidences are generally higher than the observed ones, again consistent with a protective effect of oral PrEP.
